name: Lena Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for joining me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To begin, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the data side of a payments company, the people who move money between shops and banks when you tap your card. My team builds the pipelines, basically the plumbing that carries millions of transactions into reports and fraud checks. I start around eight, check whether last night's jobs ran, then spend most of the day building new pipelines with two or three AI tools open at once.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love making something faster or cheaper and seeing the number drop on a dashboard. What wears me out is meetings where people argue about tools instead of trying them. I'm 27, I live with my partner Jonas, who's a sound engineer at a theatre, and I bought a small flat last year with savings and a bit from my grandmother. I'm fairly practical about money: index funds, a cash buffer, no drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful and the hype got ahead of itself, which happens with most new technology. At work I'd keep showing people the small time-savers that actually work. Online I'd write a short post on what AI is good for in data work and what it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I enjoy the speed. But my job is safe and my pay's good, so it's hard to complain. I'd just be very efficient at a normal job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep putting about 700 a month into index funds. I'd probably push for a senior title, since I'm already the one who knows the tools best. Maybe I'd take on a side project with a friend who runs a small online shop and needs better reporting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of restlessness. I like change, so a quiet world is fine but slightly dull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about this friend with the online shop.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Sara sells handmade ceramics online, and her sales numbers live in four different spreadsheets. I could set up a simple dashboard for her in a weekend. It wouldn't be about money, more about keeping my brain busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas's job, more than mine. Theatres are always short of money, and his contract renews every season. If the theatre loses funding, we'd be on my salary alone for a while, which we could do, but he'd hate it.

I'd keep showing colleagues the **small time-savers** that actually work.
think: My job is **safe** and my pay is good, so it's hard to complain.
I'd be a bit **disappointed**, because I enjoy the speed.
do: Keep putting about **700 a month** into index funds.
Push for a **senior title** as the team's tool expert.
Build a **weekend dashboard** for Sara's ceramics shop.
feel: **Calm**, with a little **restlessness** in a quiet world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good time to be in data, if you're willing to change how you work. At work I'd volunteer to lead whatever AI rollout the company plans. Online I'd share practical guides, not predictions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is good for me. Companies will need people who can connect AI to messy real systems, and that's basically my job. I'd worry more for colleagues who write reports by hand, because that's exactly the work that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead the AI rollout in the data team in the first quarter, and I'd ask for a raise to match. I'd keep investing and maybe up it to 1,000 a month with the raise. And I'd start doing paid weekend setups for small shops like Sara's, because that market would grow fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. I know that sounds odd, but this is the world I've been getting ready for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our reporting analyst Martin, who builds the monthly board reports by hand in spreadsheets. Martin is careful and good, but AI would do that report in minutes. I'd try to pull Martin onto checking the AI's numbers, because someone who knows what the numbers should look like is valuable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say it's good for you. What could go wrong with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company decides it needs fewer data engineers too, not just fewer analysts. I don't think that happens in this picture, but I'd keep my savings up in case. Being useful isn't the same as being safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it plainly: most desk jobs, including mine, change completely within a couple of years, so let's talk about what replaces the income. At work I'd push for us to be first, not last, so we have some say. With friends I'd be calmer than most, but more honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job as it is today ends quickly, but I might have a year or two as the person who runs the AI systems. After that, it's hard to see what an average data engineer is for. I'd be fine for money for a while, but I can't see the far side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd shift some savings out of shares into cash, because markets would go wild, and I'd overpay the flat as much as possible. I'd try to become the person who sets up AI for small businesses near us, because they'd be lost and need help. And I'd talk to Jonas about whether his hands-on theatre work could keep us going through the three years before robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan and money, but I'd know I'm guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move some money from shares into cash. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When something huge and sudden happens, prices swing hard both ways. I'd want two years of living costs in cash so I'm never forced to sell at a bad moment. The rest I'd leave invested, because the companies that own the AI might do very well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jonas say about being the steady earner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas would joke that the sound desk finally beats the laptop. Jonas rigs speakers, climbs ladders and fixes cables mid-show, which no AI does on its own. But robots come for that too around 2031, so his job is a bridge, not a home.

do: Move savings into **two years of cash** and overpay the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, and companies that start now will look after their people better. At work I'd ask for a proper plan with dates. I'd post about it, but in a practical way, like what skills to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I get three or four good years and then my current job is gone. The question is what I've built by then. I'm adaptable, so I'd rather use the time to build something of my own than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and the salary, but spend evenings turning the small-business setups into a real side business, maybe ten clients by year two. I'd keep investing, but put more into paying off the flat. By year four, I'd want the side business big enough to replace half my salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but in a determined way. It feels like a race I can actually run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Won't AI do the small-business setups too, once it's that good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, eventually, and I know it. But in the first couple of years after AGI, lots of small owners won't trust it on their own, and they'll want a person they know. I'd be that person for a while, then I'd have to change again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what's the long-term plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't fully have one, and I'd rather say so than pretend. Probably owning a share of something rather than selling my hours. My grandmother always said land and a trade, and maybe my grandmother was right about the land part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is real time, and the people who use it well will be fine. At work I'd push for training that looks past 2036, not just the next tool. With friends I'd say start now while it's cheap to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd do well for most of that decade, and my developer job would end around 2036. I'd be 37, with a paid-down flat and investments. I'm pretty sure I'd land on my feet, though the world around me might be rough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and use AI to become one of the best on my team, aiming for a senior or lead role by 2028. I'd keep investing, maybe 1,200 a month, and pay off the flat by the early 2030s. I'd also start a part-time course on running small businesses, because by 2036 I'd want to own something rather than be employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about everyone else. For me it feels like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the world around you might be rough. What do you picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Friends from university who did marketing or finance and never touched these tools. I can see some of them still doing the same job in 2034, then suddenly not. I'd try to nag them, but people don't change until it hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Jonas change any big plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about kids around 2030, once the flat is nearly paid. Ten years means we don't have to put everything on hold. I'd rather plan a family into this than around it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even with money and a plan, two years isn't enough to build anything solid. What would help is clear rules about how fast companies can cut people, and some kind of income support so the shock isn't all at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who's using the tools now. The people who'll cope best are the ones already playing with AI, and it's mostly people with spare time and money. If you're working two jobs, you don't have evenings to learn.

headlineQuote: The people who'll cope best are the ones already playing with AI, and it's mostly people with spare time and money.
